content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper tackles the problem of generating counterfactual explanations for algorithmic recourse. The authors proposed a method that works in two steps. In the first step, they train an autoencoder while constraining the latent code distribution to be close to a GMM. In the second step, a query input will be fed into the encoder, after which linear-interpolation-based search is performed in the latent space. To ensure that the three desiderata are satisfied, the authors include a label irrelevant branch, and a reconstruction loss, respectively.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength 

+ The paper is well written and well organized, with each component of the method clearly described with the accompanying Figure 1. 

+ Generating counterfactual explanations for a given model is an important problem in the ML community and also of interest to the broader audience, given its tight connection to algorithmic recourse. 

Weaknesses

- Technical merit is limited. For example, Note that Eq (1-4) are essentially a typical Gaussian linear discriminant analysis model, which essentially separately models $p(y)$ and $p(x|y)$ and uses Bayes rule to obtain $p(y|x)$, which is then used to form the classification loss. 

- Important and state-of-the-art baselines such as CounteRGAN [1] are missing. 

- There are also several issues in terms of empirical results (see below for details). 

- The paper seems incomplete, with some figures left without associated text in the main paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
One of my major concerns is that the technical merit of the proposed method is limited. Note that Eq (1-4) are essentially a typical Gaussian linear discriminant analysis model, which essentially separately models $p(y)$ and $p(x|y)$ and uses Bayes rule to obtain $p(y|x)$, which is then used to form the classification loss. Besides GMM, other techniques used (reconstruction loss and adversarial classifiers) are not new either. 

In Eq (4), should $p(\mu_{\hat{y}})$ be $p(c=\hat{y})$? 

The authors use a combination of Eq (4) and Eq (5) as the loss function for the label relevant branch. Why not directly separately train $p(c)$ and $p(z|c)$ and use the joint likelihood as the objective function? 

Another one of my major concerns is that the authors focus on the binary classification case, which is unnecessarily limiting. It would be interesting to see how the proposed method can be generalized to multi-class problems. 

Several state-of-the-art baselines on counterfactual explanations are missing, e.g., [1]. 

The paper seems incomplete. For example, Figure 2 shows some example results for MNIST. However, there is no associated text in the main paper describing the results. Besides, it is difficult to see any advantage of the proposed method compared to the listed baselines. 

The comparison in terms of reconstruction (Table 1) seems unfair. Note that in terms of CE, the reconstruction loss itself is not particularly important since it is useless to reconstruct the original query input. Therefore the fact that the reconstruction loss of the proposed method is significantly lower is not quite meaningful. 

In terms of validity, it is a bit surprising that the validity of GDL is as low as 70%, given that this is a gradient based method. A gradient based method should have done much better in steering the prediction to a specific direction. Therefore I was wondering if the comparison is fair. For example, how many iterations are used for GDL?

In terms of efficiency, note that methods like [1] only need one single feedforward pass to generate the CE and therefore should be much faster than the proposed method. Unfortunately, [1] is not included as a baseline, making it difficult to reliably evaluate the efficiency of the proposed method compared to the state of the art. 

I like Figure 1, which is a nice overview of the proposed method. It would be helpful if the authors could frequently tie the discussion back to Figure 1. 


Minor:

Page 4: Gaussian…usually in a supervised way -> do you mean ‘in an unsupervised way’?

Some pointers to figures to the Appendix are broken. 

[1] CounteRGAN: Generating Counterfactuals for Real-Time Recourse and Interpretability using Residual GANs. UAI 2022.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper tackles the problem of generating counterfactual explanations for algorithmic recourse. The authors proposed a method that works in two steps. In the first step, they train an autoencoder while constraining the latent code distribution to be close to a GMM. In the second step, a query input will be fed into the encoder, after which linear-interpolation-based search is performed in the latent space. To ensure that the three desiderata are satisfied, the authors include a label irrelevant branch, and a reconstruction loss, respectively. 

Overall the paper is well written and tackles an important problem both in the ML community and in the general ethical AI fields. My major concerns come from both limited technical merit (novelty) and inconclusive empirical results (due to missing important baselines and potentially misleading numbers).

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method of counterfactual generation to explain neural network predictions which is faster than existing methods. The innovation is learning an autoencoder with a structured latent space.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The work tackles an important problem of counterfactual generation.

An organized latent space is an intuitive way to make generating counterfactuals easier.

The method is weakened by the need for the latent representation to be trained along with the classifier. This makes the approach less versatile.

The premise that we need faster counterfactual generation is unclear to me. I do not believe that is a major challenge. Also, the experiments involve the very small MNIST dataset so this does not really demonstrate scalability.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
While the method potentially can generate nice counterfactuals that are actionable I do not feel these experiments demonstrated this Experiments in these related works: xGEMs (https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.08867) and Latent Shift (https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.09475) used more intuitive graphical datasets to demonstrate the fidelity and actionability of the counterfactuals generated. Experiments on MNIST are not compelling because it is hard to distinguish how well each method removes the features of a '7' from an image because they all look similar. 

There is a statement in the paper "Our method outperforms Prototype and RL in the time dimension since it searches through the latent space with lower dimensions" which I don't understand to be true. The method uses known centroids to limit the steps of the search right? The dimensionality of the latent space is not a factor as all methods can use the same size latent space.

The work also argues that their method "provides more valid CEs which are closer to the original dataset" which is measured by "the percentage success in generating CEs that the target labels requested by the users are reached". This is a very interesting metric which I have not seen before and I find very valuable because when these methods fail they fail very hard and create nonsense counterfactuals. I wish the authors dove more into this with more experiments. The method proposed essentially guarantees that you will end up in a known centroid of another class so I don't see why this would not be 100% unless some of the centroids are not correctly predicted. One thing that is not accounted for here is when a nonsense counterfactual is generated that could change the classifiers prediction.
content.summary_of_the_review: While this work presents a clear goal to speed up counterfactual generation I do not see that as a major concern to address. This work explores a structured latent space but the evaluation is too simple and is not compelling compared to evaluations in related work. Also, for this aspect, other approaches for feature disentanglement are not explored so it is also not compelling. For these reasons I do not recommend acceptance.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to leverage the auto-encoder, GMM and adversarial training to obtain a counterfactual generator. The trained model aims to explain a pre-trained classifier by linear interpolation in the latent space. The method is demonstrated on MNIST, Adult Income and LCD.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1) It combines generative modeling, GMM and adversarial training together for generating counterfactuals. 
2) It can be applied to tabular data sets as demonstrated in the experiment. 

Weaknesses:
1) There isn't much novelty in manipulating the latent space of the auto-encoder. 
2) The demonstrated MNIST examples are not promising and intriguing. Actually, many papers can achieve even better results[1,2,3]. Thus, I am concerned about the effectiveness of the proposed method. 




1. Pawelczyk, M., Broelemann, K., & Kasneci, G. (2020, April). Learning model-agnostic counterfactual explanations for tabular data. In Proceedings of The Web Conference 2020 (pp. 3126-3132).

2. Downs, M., Chu, J. L., Yacoby, Y., Doshi-Velez, F., & Pan, W. (2020). Cruds: Counterfactual recourse using disentangled subspaces. ICML WHI, 2020, 1-23.

3. Zhang, W., Barr, B., & Paisley, J. (2022, November). An Interpretable Deep Classifier for Counterfactual Generation. In 3rd ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (pp. 36-43).
